The operation was halted only after officials discovered the report's inaccuracies, which were traced to a chatbot that misidentified the ship's cargo, highlighting risks in relying on AI for critical military intelligence.

The report originated from a US Special Operations Command analyst who used AI tools combining open-source and classified intelligence to produce the false findings. This incident occurred amid the military's broader push to integrate AI across various functions, including intelligence analysis and battlefield decision-making, despite concerns about inconsistent verification standards and potential for catastrophic errors. The episode underscores the dangers of rapid AI adoption in high-stakes environments without robust safeguards.

items.originalTitle: How To Write With An LLM
items.summary: Thomas Ptacek recommends using large language models (LLMs) only for copyediting tasks such as fact-checking, spelling, and grammar, while avoiding adopting any specific phrases they suggest. He argues that this approach serves as intellectual personal protective equipment, helping writers maintain discipline and avoid the characteristic "weird smell" of AI-generated text. Ptacek shares his personal LLM copyediting tool and provides prompts to help others build similar systems, emphasizing the importance of not letting LLMs write original content for his blog.

items.originalSummary:
How To Write With An LLM

Thomas Ptacek on using LLMs as copyeditors, not as writing assistants:

Rule Number One: You may not use a single word an LLM suggests to you.

[...] I think that as a form of intellectual personal protective equipment you should adopt the rule that any specific turn of phrase an LLM suggests is off limits. Be strict about the rule!

I won't let LLMs write content for my blog, but I use them for fact-checking, spelling and grammar and as an occasional thesaurus (see my proofreading prompt).

The rule to never use a turn of phrase suggested by an LLM feels good to me. The text has that weird smell to it, and it's also a good principle to help stay disciplined.

Later in this piece Thomas shows a screenshot of his personal LLM copyediting tool (see also this Twitter thread), and provides a prompt to help kickstart building your own.

Update: Thomas also shared his system prompt in a comment on Hacker News.

items.title: Researchers find human brain develops from two distinct neural progenitor cell types, reflecting ancient dual nervous system origins
items.originalTitle: Two parallel neural ectoderm progenitors contribute to the developing brain
items.summary:
Researchers at Stanford University discovered that the human brain develops from two separate types of neural progenitor cells, with one type forming the forebrain and midbrain and the other forming the hindbrain. This finding challenges previous assumptions that the brain regions share a common developmental origin and suggests the brain evolved by merging two primitive nervous systems.

The team studied mouse embryos and human cells in vitro, confirming the distinct origins of brain regions and enabling the first successful growth of functional human hindbrain motor neurons in a dish. This advance may aid research into diseases affecting the hindbrain, such as ALS and spinal muscular atrophy, and improve understanding of how certain appetite-suppressing drugs work. The dual-origin brain system appears to have evolved at least 550 million years ago, potentially facilitating complex brain functions by allowing the forebrain to develop independently from basic life-sustaining processes managed by the hindbrain.

items.title: Agentgit launches a Git hosting service for AI agents with no accounts or tokens required, featuring append-only refs and automatic repository deletion after 24 hours [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Agentgit – a Git host for AI agents, no account, no token, no key
items.summary:
Agentgit has introduced a Git hosting platform designed for AI agents that requires no user accounts, tokens, or keys. Repositories are created automatically on the first push, are world-readable by default, and support append-only refs to prevent history rewriting or deletion. The service deletes repositories 24 hours after their last push, making it suitable as temporary scratch space.

The platform enforces size limits on pushes and repositories, rate limits per client, and allows signed pushes to credit contributors. Users can watch for new pushes via a WebSocket-based notification system. Pushes are refused if they attempt to rewrite history or use an already taken repository name, with clear error messages guiding users to resolve issues.

items.originalTitle: A startup that builds other startups raised $100M, and is all-in on physical AI
items.summary:
Vantora, formerly UP.Labs, secured $100 million from Silversmith Capital Partners to focus on creating startups that develop physical AI solutions for industrial corporations, including clients in manufacturing and oil and gas. The company builds ventures tailored to its corporate partners, who can invest in and integrate these startups into their core businesses, keeping the innovations proprietary.

Since its launch in 2022 with Porsche as its first partner, Vantora has expanded its client base to include Alaska Airlines, J.B. Hunt, Wabash, and TDG. The shift to a proprietary M&A pipeline allows Vantora to pursue sensitive projects that address significant operational challenges, such as retrofitting hardware for autonomy, which corporate partners prefer to keep exclusive rather than commercialize broadly.

Led by CEO Diogo Almeida, a former OpenAI researcher, Jev processes data in parallel to produce type-safe, calibrated outputs without generating free-form text, aiming to reduce costs and latency in agent pipelines.

Jev reportedly operates up to 193.6 times faster and 444.6 times cheaper than leading LLMs in internal tests, with latency measured in milliseconds and pricing significantly lower per decision. However, its capabilities are limited to predefined output schemas and structured tasks, excluding code generation or conversational abilities. The company’s benchmarks compare Jev’s accuracy to other AI models rather than independent ground truth, and it remains in early access without disclosed production customers or revenue.

TypeSafe positions Jev as a modular component for AI agent stacks, handling high-frequency, low-complexity decisions while reserving LLMs for complex reasoning tasks. The company’s $40 million seed funding and $200 million valuation reflect investor confidence in this architectural approach, though broader validation and adoption are still pending.

items.originalTitle: Communicate Technical Topics to a Non-Technical Audience with Google Gemini
items.summary:
In a room full of IT professionals, words and phrases like “tokenization,” “retrieval-augmented generation,” and “context window” need no explanation. But when technology leaders present to their CEOs and other company leaders about topics like AI, they often find that they need to translate these terms into everyday business language, or else risk being met by blank stares.

In the moment, this can be maddening. You know the opportunities and challenges that a technology like generative AI presents for your company. And you know that the organization’s other leaders will likely see things the same way you do, if only you can make yourself understood.

Instead of trying to bridge this communication gap on the fly, use Google Gemini to help translate your technical vision into bottom-line business value.

Step 1: Figure Out What You Want to Say

Your CEO might not speak “tech,” but Google Gemini does. Open up a new chat and explain exactly what it is you hope to communicate to leadership. Here, you can feel free to be as technical as you wish. Maybe you’ll tell Gemini that you’re thinking of building a RAG pipeline to vectorize your company’s proprietary data. Or, maybe you’ll float the idea of using parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA to deploy open-weight models on-premises, without exploding your cloud inference costs. You can even upload your technical documents to Gemini, directly in the chat window.

No matter how in-the-weeds you get, Gemini will follow your train of thought, parsing the complexity to find the business value at the core of your plans.

Step 2: Let Gemini Be Your Translator

Now that you’ve captured your vision in your own words, let Gemini help you translate those words into language that will connect with your audience. Use this sample prompt, along with your brainstorming from Step 1:

I am the CIO at [company], and I am trying to build the case to [adopt generative AI solutions]. I need to explain the technical concept of generative AI to a non-technical audience (the CEO and board). Help me write talking points that will help me convey what generative AI is, ways it could help us digitally transform, and why it’s important to our growth as a company. Include details about how it could potentially re-focus our technical talent on more strategic work, help enhance our workforce’s productivity, and help us better serve our global workforce and customers.

In just a few moments, you’ll have a set of boardroom-ready talking points. Gemini might, for instance, break down the benefits of RAG in simple terms by noting that it anchors AI to internal data like HR policies and technical manuals. Or, it might point out the business benefits of arming IT staff and engineers with generative AI tools, noting the opportunity to shift employees’ focus from low-value, repetitive tasks to innovation.

Step 3: Create Content


Now that you have your core narrative and language nailed down, Gemini can help you create a more structured pitch. Instead of staring at a blank slide deck, prompt Gemini for ideas on how to build out a presentation that will sway your peers in the C-suite. Try this prompt:

I need to build a presentation to deliver this information to the board. Turn these talking points into a 10-slide presentation. For each slide, write a headline, three to four short bullet points for the slide itself, and the speaker notes I should use to explain the concept out loud.

Gemini will generate a full, downloadable presentation deck directly in the chat. If you like, you can export the presentation to Google Slides and make your own edits. Or, you can command Gemini to generate a new version with changes to elements like design, language, and narrative flow.

Step 4: Make Gemini Your Sparring Partner

Before you go into your meeting, open a new chat in Gemini, providing your speaker notes and a link to your presentation, and then ask it to act as a skeptical executive: You are my CEO. Review this presentation and grill me on cost, security, and ROI. Ask your toughest questions, one at a time.

Even though Gemini helped you prepare your presentation, it will seamlessly pivot to the role of rigorous executive or tough board member, pressing for more details on project payback, hidden risks, and timeline. By practicing your pitch in this low-stakes environment, you can make certain that you’ll be confident when it’s time for the real thing.
